title: Live TV-radio coverage, first time ever
primary_topics: The SC June 14, 2011 resolution -- the first ever -- allowing live TV/radio broadcast of a criminal case (the Ampatuan multiple murder case) pro hac vice
The historical evolution from absolute ban (1991 Cory Aquino libel case, 2001 Estrada plunder case) to the first-ever live coverage authorization
CJ 2001 dissent advocating a single fixed camera under court control -- and the vindication of that technology-based approach in the 2011 resolution
sub_topics: SC resolution dated June 14, 2011 (written by Justice Conchita Carpio Morales): unanimous; granted pro hac vice live TV-radio coverage of Ampatuan multiple murder case; first time ever
Historical absolute ban: Oct. 22, 1991 -- unanimous ban on live coverage of Cory Aquino libel case; citing US SCOTUS Estes v. Texas (5-4, forbidding TV cameras in criminal trials)

Estrada plunder case ban: June 29, 2001 resolution (J. Vitug), 8-6 with one on leave -- flatly denied live TV-radio coverage; prejudice to due process and orderly administration of justice; right to information satisfied by less distracting means
Estrada subsequent resolution (Sept. 13, 2001): relaxed ban and allowed cameras for documentary purposes (not live, real-time broadcast)

CJ 2001 dissent: joined minority opposing total ban; proposed single fixed camera under court control feeding audio-visual output to wide TV monitors inside and outside courtroom; TV and radio crews beam output to stations without intimidating wiring/lights/cameras inside courthouse; cameras locked to wide-angle stationary audience view -- no panning, focusing, angling

Rationale for 2011 pro hac vice ruling: unique circumstances -- 57 victim families, 197 accused, over 200 prosecution witnesses + 200 defense witnesses; physically impossible to accommodate even the parties in courtroom; technology is the only solution

2011 guidelines: (1) single fixed compact camera installed inconspicuously, no panning/zooming, wide-angle full view; (2) media companies interconnected with least physical disturbance; (3) broadcasting must be continuous and in entirety; no commercial breaks except during recess; no voice-over; annotations observe sub judice rule
Concern: continuous coverage without commercial breaks very expensive and may dampen TV participation
CJ welcome: recognizes the view from his 2001 dissent that technology can give Filipinos in their homes the same access as spectators inside the courthouse
signature_phrases: Finally and at last, the Supreme Court allowed... the live TV-radio coverage of a criminal case
first time that the highest court has authorized the live broadcast of a courtroom drama

stances.claim: The SC June 14, 2011 resolution authorizing pro hac vice live TV/radio coverage of the Ampatuan case is the first-ever authorization in SC history, correctly grounded in the unique circumstances: physical impossibility of accommodating all parties -- making technology the only solution for a transparent, open and public trial.

The 2011 resolution validates CJ 2001 dissent: a single fixed camera under court control, locked to wide-angle stationary view, feeding audio-visual output to monitors inside and outside the courthouse -- the technologically feasible solution respecting accused rights and trial dignity.

The requirement of continuous coverage without commercial breaks may be a dampener for TV companies, but the resolution is still welcome for recognizing the public right to the same access as courtroom spectators.
stances.rhetorical_move: qualified-welcome (acknowledges commercial-break limitation while celebrating the breakthrough)

notable_anecdotes: The 10-year gap between CJ 2001 minority dissent proposing a single fixed camera and the 2011 unanimous resolution that effectively adopted the same approach -- a decade of vindication in a single SC resolution.

The three-case historical arc: 1991 Cory Aquino libel (unanimous total ban citing Estes v. Texas) to 2001 Estrada plunder (8-6 total ban, then documentary cameras) to 2011 Ampatuan (unanimous first-ever live coverage pro hac vice) -- the SC 20-year evolution from absolute prohibition to technological embrace.

The physical impossibility of accommodating 57 victim families, 197 accused, 20+ sets of lawyers, 200+ prosecution and defense witnesses as the specific factual predicate that finally unlocked the live coverage door.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban celebrates the SC's June 14, 2011 resolution (written by Justice Conchita Carpio Morales, unanimous) as the first time the Supreme Court has ever authorized live TV/radio coverage of a criminal case -- granting it pro hac vice for the Ampatuan multiple murder case. He traces the historical arc of the absolute ban: in 1991, the Court unanimously denied live coverage of the Cory Aquino libel case (citing Estes v. Texas, where the US SCOTUS banned TV cameras 5-4); in 2001, the 8-6 Estrada plunder resolution (J. Vitug) flatly denied live coverage on due process and fair-administration grounds, with a subsequent resolution allowing only documentary cameras. CJ discloses that in 2001 he was a sitting justice who joined the minority: he proposed a single fixed camera under court control, locked to wide-angle stationary view, feeding audio-visual output to wide TV monitors inside and outside the courthouse -- enabling TV and radio crews to broadcast without intimidating media equipment inside. The 2011 resolution adopted precisely this approach. It was justified by the Ampatuan case's unique circumstances: 57 victim families, 197 accused, over 200 prosecution and defense witnesses -- physical impossibility of accommodating all parties makes technology the only solution for a transparent, open and public trial. CJ notes the continuous-coverage-without-commercial-break requirement may dampen TV participation but welcomes the resolution as recognizing that technology can give Filipinos in their homes the same access as courtroom spectators.
